analysis.one_liner: Raises the estate tax exemption to $10 million per person and indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from March 2000 until Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have phased in a much larger estate tax exemption, rising from $5 million in 2000 to $10 million by 2003, with the amount growing with inflation afterward [S2][S3]. Estates below that amount would pay no federal estate or gift tax at all. It would also repeal a separate, smaller tax break for family-owned business interests, since the larger general exemption would cover more of those cases [S3]. Because only estates worth millions of dollars owe estate tax, the money saved would go almost entirely to the heirs of the wealthiest families, while the federal government would collect less revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of very large estates. The federal estate tax already exempts the first several million dollars of an estate and applies only to estates at the top of the wealth distribution, so raising the exemption to $10 million and indexing it delivers its savings to a small number of the wealthiest families. Very large family farms and businesses would also gain, and estate owners would no longer need the separate family-business deduction the bill repeals.

how_it_helps.text: The bill phases in an exemption of $5 million in 2000, $6.75 million in 2001, $8.5 million in 2002, and $10 million in 2003 and after, so estates below those levels would owe no estate or gift tax [S3].
After 2003 the $10 million exemption would rise each year with inflation, so the tax-free threshold would grow over time rather than being eroded by rising asset values [S2][S3].
It repeals the separate, smaller exclusion for family-owned business interests, replacing it with the much larger general exemption [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and therefore taxpayers generally. Every dollar of estate tax the exemption eliminates is revenue the government must replace with other taxes, more borrowing, or less spending. The burden falls broadly while the benefit is concentrated among the heirs of the largest estates.

drawbacks.text: The revenue loss is the central cost: the estate tax falls only on the largest estates, so a $10 million exemption converts most of what it now collects into lost federal revenue, which must be made up through other taxes, borrowing, or reduced spending [S2][S3].

Because the exemption phases in at $5 million immediately and applies to deaths after December 31, 2000, the savings go exclusively to families whose estates are already worth several million dollars or more; households with no estate-tax exposure receive nothing [S3].

Repealing the family-owned business exclusion could leave some business owners worse off in narrow cases where the old special deduction was worth more than the new general exemption, though the bill's larger general exemption is designed to cover those situations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it removes a tax from multi-million-dollar estates and simplifies planning for family businesses. The cost is broad: federal revenue that everyone else effectively makes up. Weighing a concentrated gain against a diffuse public cost, the design favors the wealthiest families.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late March 2000 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Ewing introduced the bill on March 29, 2000, with 40 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S4][S5].
The committee took no further action; the record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury, and taxpayers generally, kept the estate tax revenue that a $10 million exemption would have eliminated. The bill's sponsor and cosponsors gained nothing from its failure, and heirs of large estates continued to owe the tax at existing exemption levels.

for.name: Rep. Thomas W. Ewing
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the estate tax exemption to $10 million and index it to inflation.

for.name: 41 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship but a heavily Republican base.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the nine months it had jurisdiction, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Of the 41 cosponsors, 39 were Republicans and 2 were Democrats; no floor vote ever occurred to test broader support [S4].

industries.industry: Heirs and estates of the wealthiest households
industries.note: The bill died, so large estates continue to owe estate tax at existing exemption levels. Had it passed, its benefits would have gone almost entirely to families with estates worth several million dollars or more.

industries.industry: Estate planning services and life insurers selling estate-tax coverage
industries.note: Had the exemption risen to $10 million and beyond, far fewer estates would have needed estate-tax planning or life insurance held to cover the tax. The bill's death keeps that market intact.

The bill would have replaced the special family-business exclusion with a much larger general exemption, letting more family farms and businesses pass without tax. Most such estates were already below existing exemption levels, so the practical gain was limited to the larger ones.
